title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
abstract: Evaluations are critical for understanding language model capabilities. This article introduces statistical thinking into language model evaluations, providing formulas for analyzing evaluation data and measuring differences between models.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content:
Imagine you're comparing two language models, Galleon and Dreadnought, on three evaluations: MATH, HumanEval, and MGSM. The results show conflicting performances: Galleon outperforms Dreadnought on MATH, but Dreadnought performs better on HumanEval and MGSM. How can you determine which model is truly better?

This is where statistical analysis comes in. By adding error bars to evaluation results, you can quantify the uncertainty associated with each model's performance.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
To analyze evaluation data, we can use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to estimate the standard error of the mean. The CLT states that the distribution of sample means will be approximately normal, even if the underlying data is not. We can use this to compute the standard error of the mean, which represents the uncertainty associated with our estimate of the model's performance.

For example, if we have 5,000 questions in the MATH evaluation, and the standard error of the mean is 0.7%, we can report the result as 65.5% ± 0.7%.

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content:
Let's look at some real-world benchmark results. Table 2 shows the results of the MATH, HumanEval, and MGSM evaluations, along with the standard error of each estimate. We can see that the standard error is relatively small for the MATH evaluation, but larger for the HumanEval and MGSM evaluations.

This suggests that the MATH evaluation is more precise, while the HumanEval and MGSM evaluations are less precise.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Adding error bars to evaluation results is crucial for understanding the uncertainty associated with each model's performance. By reporting the standard error of the mean, we can quantify the precision of our estimates and make more informed decisions.

For example, if we want to determine whether the difference between two models is statistically significant, we can use the standard error to compute a confidence interval.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content:
This article presents several key innovations for analyzing evaluation data. First, we introduce the concept of clustered standard errors, which account for the dependence between questions in an evaluation. Second, we show how to reduce the variance of estimates using resampling and next-token probabilities.

Finally, we provide a sample-size formula for determining the number of questions required to achieve a given level of precision.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content:
To apply these concepts to your own evaluation data, you can use the formulas and techniques presented in this article. For example, you can use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate the standard error of the mean, and then compute a confidence interval to determine whether the difference between two models is statistically significant.

You can also use the sample-size formula to determine the number of questions required to achieve a given level of precision.
